text: Owl pellets: a wise DNA source for small mammal genetics

Pellets of raptors are an important source for the study of the taxonomy, phylogeography and ecological diversity of small vertebrates. Since birds of prey are efficient collecting agents for both rare species and those reluctant to enter traps, they offer an important complement to traditional trapping efforts in the field. The possibility of using bones and teeth recovered from pellets as a convenient alternative DNA source for genetic studies requires a more complete understanding of the DNA preservation of these partially digested remains. It is not yet clear, for example, to which degree DNA is preserved and how heterogeneous DNA preservation is in the different skeletal remains found in pellets since systematic quantitative analyses are missing. Here, we attempt to improve this knowledge by quantifying the degradation of DNA during the digestion process of raptors using 62 individual rodent bones and teeth from different pellets. We show a very high variability in DNA preservation between bones. Interestingly, variability between bones within the same pellet is much higher than that found between pellets, which has major consequences for genetic studies as it implies that bones from the same pellet that could belong to different individuals/species should be tested individually when multiple markers are analyzed. We find that neither the identity of the skeletal part nor microscopic observation of the degree of digestion are useful proxies for DNA preservation, and we thus recommend the use of screening strategies to identify the most suitable bones to include in analyses. We conclude that pellets of owls, whether freshly collected or from natural history collections, can be a practical noninvasive source for genetic studies of small vertebrates provided the design of the study takes into account the short DNA molecule length, the low quantity of DNA preserved and the heterogeneity in DNA preservation.

Rodents are important factors in all terrestrial ecosystems because of their high biomass, the richness of species and the ecological roles they play as prey, seed dispersers and invasive species. There are three sources for the study of the ecology, phylogeny and taxonomy of rodents: (1) live animals, (2) natural history collections and (3) pellets of birds of prey. Of these, pellets provide different information than can be obtained from field studies and natural history collections, making them an important complementary DNA source for biodiversity studies. In particular, birds of prey capture a higher diversity of rodents, and of microvertebrates in general, than researchers since they also capture rare species and those which avoid trapping and are therefore underrepresented in live and natural history collections (e.g. Torre, Arrizabalaga & Flaquer, 2004, as well as unpublished observations by CD). Since raptors offer to researchers the bones of their prey in regurgitated pellets, birds of prey play a useful role in studies aiming to deepen the knowledge of the ecology and phylogeography of the various microvertebrate species (e.g. Bock, Jones & Bock, 2007). These pellets are formed in the bird's gizzard and contain the indigestible parts, that is, bones, teeth, fur, feathers, beaks and claws of animals that have been ingested whole. The pellet then moves to the proventriculus, where it will remain for roughly 8 h (sometimes up to 24), before being regurgitated (Grimm & Whitehouse, 1963;Andrews, 1990). If the owl swallows multiple animals within several hours, the various remains are consolidated into a single pellet, so that each pellet may contain several individuals from different species (Dodson & Wexlar, 1979). The degree of digestion depends on the acidity of the gastric juices, the quantity of pancreatic juice sometimes entering the stomach by reflux and neutralizing the gastric content (Leprince, Dandrifosse & Schoffeniels, 1979), and the time before regurgitation (Raczynski & Ruprecht, 1974;Andrews, 1990). Strigiformes, in particular barn owls, digest their prey to a lesser extent than do the other birds of prey (notably Falconiformes), and thus owl pellets contain a larger amount of skeletal remains, generally being less digested (Raczynski & Ruprecht, 1974;Andrews, 1990). Additionally, the pellets may contain several individuals, which allows the simultaneous recovery of different species from different habitats within the hunting territory of the bird of prey. Therefore, the use of owl pellets as a source for the analysis of microvertebrates has the advantage of being both non-invasive (there is no need to kill or trap living organisms) and an efficient sampling technique. Because of these characteristics, pellets have been used for taxonomic, phylogeographic, biogeographic, ecological, environmental and taphonomic studies of small mammals both from modern and fossil assemblages (e.g. Mikkola, 1983;Andrews, 1990). Finally, most fossil microvertebrate assemblages, in particular cave accumulations, result from accumulated pellets of raptors or feces of carnivores (e.g. Mellett, 1974;Mayhew, 1977;Andrews, 1990).
Despite the fact that pellets offer unique insights to taxonomic and phylogeographic studies, few studies have used them as a source for the genotyping of skeletal material (Taberlet & Fumagalli, 1996;Jaarola & Searle, 2004;Poulakakis et al., 2005;Bus et al., 2014). In particular, systematic quantitative studies are missing to define the extent of their potential for genetic studies. First, the degree to which DNA is preserved in the bones and teeth of the prey species and how heterogeneous this preservation is among individual remains has yet to be explored. Indeed, DNA is readily degraded through acidic hydrolysis leading to depurination and DNA fragmentation (Lindahl & Nyberg, 1972) and the gastric juices of the raptors are highly acidic (Duke et al., 1975;Leprince et al., 1979). Furthermore, different genetic analysis strategies must be developed depending on the extent of heterogeneity of DNA preservation. For instance, substantial differential DNA preservation between bones of the same pellet could create serious challenges for the genetic studies of multiple genetic markers on independent DNA fragments, such as when using multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR), single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) arrays or next-generation sequencing. Since pellets can contain bones from different individuals from the same or different species, it is important to know whether bones from each individual pellet can be analyzed in pools while allowing genotype coordination if more than one individual contributes to the data, or if they should be analyzed individually. If bones must be analyzed individually, the optimal type and number of bones that should be analyzed to ensure the most efficient and non-biased data collection must be determined. Thus, in order to understand how broadly such genetic studies can be applied to skeletal material from pellets and what are the optimal parameters for the success of such studies, several important questions remain to be addressed:
(1) how much DNA is degraded through the bird's digestion process and what is the average size of the DNA molecules? (2) Is there a difference in the DNA degradation in different types of skeletal remains? (3) Is the DNA degradation process homogeneous throughout the pellets and between different pellets from the same predator as well as between different predators whose digestion is more or less harsh?
Here, we address these important questions by performing an in-depth quantitative study of DNA degradation in bones and teeth from owl pellets using both sensitive genetic techniques and microscopy to better understand the extent to which DNA degradation of skeletal material in pellets is impacted by the variability of this digestion process, as evidenced by length and quantity of remaining DNA content as well as the structural damage at the individual bone level. We assessed particularly the intra-pellet variability of DNA survival in rodent bones using several pellets originating from the same area to minimize other potential sources of heterogeneity. These pellets originate from northwest Africa, an area known for its rich species diversity (Aulagnier & Thévenot, 1986) that to our knowledge has not yet been investigated in terms of biogeography and phylogeography of small mammals using this approach. We used quantitative PCR (qPCR) and a DNA degradation model (Deagle, Eveson & Jarman, 2006) to determine the extent of DNA degradation, the average length of the remaining DNA and the bone-tobone variability both within a single pellet and between different pellets. We targeted mitochondrial DNA as a proxy for DNA preservation because its high copy number allows more reliable quantitative measurements. Furthermore, we used electron microscopy to analyze the degree and type of histological degradation caused by gastric digestion of the bird of prey to establish if it is correlated to DNA degradation.

We analyzed four pellets from different sites in Central Morocco, that is, Berrechid, Mechra Benabbou, Ouled Boughadi and Sidi Chiker collected between 1984 and 2010 (Table 1). The pellet collected in 1984 in the surroundings of Sidi Chiker, was produced by a long-eared owl (Asio otus), and has been stored since collection in a university office in Toulouse, France. The other pellets were collected during field missions for small vertebrate trapping in 2010 and 2011. The pellets from Berrechid were collected in 2010 from the top of a tower at a research station of the Scientific Institute of Rabat. The predator producing these pellet accumulations was not identified directly, but according to the physical aspect of the pellets and the observations made, it was probably a barn owl (Tyto alba). The pellets from Mechra Benabbou were collected in 2010 during herpetological surveys, and come from an unidentified avian predator (probably a small owl). A falcon pellet (Falco tinnunuculus) had been collected in Ouled Boughadi in April 2011.

section: conservation and preparation of the pellets
text:
After collection, the pellets were sealed in plastic bags (Minigrip Zip Pak) and placed in a refrigerator upon return from the field mission in order to limit insect development and pellet deterioration. Prey remains were separated from the rest of the pellets using forceps in workstations that were ultraviolet (UV)-irradiated, and frequently wiped with bleach to decontaminate surfaces and equipment.
Several anatomical parts were included in the analysis (femur, tibia, mandibles, skull, molars and incisors; Table 1), totaling 62 independent bones and teeth.

The identification of rodent bones was performed under a binocular microscope (by E.S.). Species identification was based on morphology and size of skulls and molars through comparison with osteological collections at the National History Museum of Paris using identification keys (e.g. Aulagnier & Thévenot, 1986;Barreau, Rocher & Aulagnier, 1991). Species attribution is more difficult in the case of postcranial long bones and was mainly based on size (i.e. largest ones were assigned to Meriones). The list of the samples and sample names can be found in Supporting Information Table 1.

For the microscopic analysis, a previously described procedure was followed (Andrews, 1990). In this way, anatomical identification, degrees of gastric digestion (from light to extreme) and degrees of breakage of skeletal remains were recorded, as well as other structural modifications related to the environment of deposition (e.g. cracking, insect damage). For the collection as a whole, a variable magnification (×10 to ×80) of the light microscope has been used. Long bones and mandibles (with or without teeth) were cut transversally with an electrical saw and one half was observed under a low vacuum or environmental scanning electron microscope (ESEM) of the Museo de Ciencias Naturales in Madrid, Spain. The other half was not subject to SEM analysis but only to DNA analysis to prevent potential DNA damage due to X-ray emission when exposed to electrons. Surface observations were done in backscattered electron mode, combined with secondary electron emission mode, at 20-30 kV, 0.6-0.33 Torr. This new generation of ESEMs enables specimens to be directly analyzed at high magnification and high resolution without coating or any other pretreatment. After surface analysis, samples were prepared for histological observations by immersing them in resin and polishing the surface with different abrasive grains of silicon carbide powder and dis-tilled water and finally with a diamond saw of 3-1 microns. Histological analyses were performed in backscattered electron (BSE-SEM) mode.

The experimental procedures were performed in workstations that were UV-irradiated. Surfaces and equipment were frequently cleaned with bleach. The samples recovered from the pellets were weighed and suspended in 1 mL of DNA extraction buffer containing 0.5M EDTA, 0.25M disodium hydrogen phosphate (Na2HPO4) pH 8.0, 0.14 M 2-mercaptoethanol, 2% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) and 0.5 mg mL -1 of proteinase K. This enzymatic digestion was performed at 50°C under agitation until complete dissolution of teeth and bones. Negative extraction controls were performed for each extraction. DNA was purified using the Qiaquick PCR Purification Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany), according to the manufacturer's protocol.

For the comparison of the DNA quantity that is lost during the digestion process in the raptor's stomach, we used as a reference sample fresh skeletal parts from a modern specimen of Mus musculus, raised in an animal facility and not subjected to digestion by birds of prey. The mouse was dissected immediately after euthanasia in a physically separated laboratory to avoid contamination of the pellet extracts with modern mouse DNA. The bones were defleshed mechanically with a scalpel, followed by an additional defleshing step performed by digesting each sample individually for 1 h at 50°C in digestion buffer (Tris 100 mM pH8, NaCl 150 mM, 1% N-lauroyl-sarcosyl) with 5 mg mL -1 of proteinase K. The buffer was discarded and the bones and teeth dried on sterile towels, weighed and resuspended in 1 mL of 0.5 M EDTA, 0.25M disodium hydrogen phosphate (Na2HPO4) pH 8.0, 0.14 M 2-mercaptoethanol, 2% SDS and 0.5 mg mL -1 of proteinase K at 50°C under agitation until complete dissolution of teeth and bones.
We performed an alignment of all complete mtDNA sequences of rodents available in the Genbank database and targeted genome regions conserved among all rodent species

The extracts were tested for inhibition with the real-time PCR Lightcycler 2.0, Roche Applied Science, Penzberg, Germany, using 20 pg genomic M. musculus DNA as a reference and the primer pair 73F/73R, as previously described (Pruvost & Geigl 2004;Pruvost et al. 2007). The amplifications were performed in a 384-well plate allowing for small reaction volumes (7 μL) in the real-time PCR Lightcycler 480 system, Roche Applied Science. The PCR amplifications were carried out in a reaction volume of 7 μL by mixing 2 μL of extract with 5 μL of a premix containing Light Cycler 480 SYBR Green I Master Mix 1× and primers (0.5 μM). The cycling program consisted of 5 min of activation at 95°C followed by 50 cycles at 95°C for 10 s and 60°C for 1 min, with a final melting curve determination. We performed five amplification replicates for each extract and for each primer pair. Several negative controls were done for each PCR.

section: estimation of average dna molecule length
text:
The strategy used to determine DNA degradation was based on the rationale that DNA degradation occurs randomly and follows a first-order kinetics. According to a model of random degradation, the amount of available template should decline exponentially with increasing molecule size in damaged samples. DNA damage is expected to occur according to a random Poisson process at a rate of λ per nucleotide (i.e. λ is the probability of a nucleotide being damaged). The resulting size distribution of undamaged molecules (x) is defined by an exponential distribution with parameter λ:
where Ax is the number of amplifiable copies of size x and N is the total number of DNA copies. It follows from the properties of an exponential distribution that the average size of undamaged DNA molecules is 1/λ (Deagle et al., 2006). To estimate the average DNA molecule size, the amount of DNA molecules detectable with amplicons of 73, 125 and 158 bp was quantified using qPCR using as a reference modern, high molecular weight M. musculus DNA. Since we expected DNA to be degraded, we targeted small amplicons to ensure reliable estimation of very small molecules. The average quantity of DNA molecules was then plotted against the amplicon length (bp). The average molecule length (1/λ) was determined using the slope of the regression exponential curve (-λ). Figure 1 a shows a typical quantification experiment that reveals the performance and simplicity of this strategy.

Of the 55 bones and teeth extracted from only the owl pellets, 10 failed to amplify at least the two largest amplicons. None of the extracts inhibited the PCR as assessed by quantification of added reporter DNA using PCR. Of the 10 samples that failed to amplify the two largest fragments (125 and 158 bp), nine contained low amounts of DNA molecules long enough to allow amplification of the shortest (73 bp) amplicon, that is, ranging from 30 000 to 660 000 molecules per gram of bone. One sample of these 10 yielded no amplification product even for the 73 bp amplicon. Of the 45 samples that amplified all three fragments, the amount of DNA molecules in the pellet samples that were at least 73 bp long (i.e. the minimal size necessary to amplify the smallest amplicon) ranged between one million and hundred million molecules per gram of bone/ tooth corresponding to a loss of DNA of 90-99.9% (median of 99%) compared with the reference bones from the freshly killed mouse (Fig. 1b). Using the values obtained for the three fragments, we quantified the average DNA molecule size for these 45 samples to be between 11 and 1429 bp (Fig. 1b), including four outliers with an average DNA molecule length larger than 1000 bp, a size range that can only be considered as an estimate since the short amplicons used do not accurately measure the size of molecules that are much larger than their own size. In 85% of the bones, the average DNA molecule size is below 200 bp. Thus, both the average DNA quantity and fragment size varies between bones by two orders of magnitude. Strikingly, there was no correlation between the number of amplifiable molecules ≥73 bp and the average size of DNA molecules (Fig. 1b). Not a single correlation plot (linear, exponential, logarithmic, polynomial) yielded a goodness of fit R 2 value above 0.1. Furthermore, the quantity of DNA recovered varied by two orders of magnitude for fragments whose average size was smaller than 200 bp, and both the highest and smallest DNA quantity were represented among bone extracts that yielded the smallest average DNA fragment size (<50 bp).

We first explored whether the bone-to-bone variability could be due to differences between pellets. The variation in DNA degradation between the three owl pellets from the same geographical origin was much lower than the bone-to-bone variability that was found within the individual pellets. The median size of DNA molecules and the median DNA content were 100 bp and 11.3 million molecules per gram, respectively, in the extracts from the bones of the pellet from Sidi Chiker, 167 bp and 5.4 million molecules per gram, respectively, in the extracts from the bones of the pellet from Mechra Benabbou, and 111 bp and 3.9 million molecules per gram, respectively, in the extracts from the bones of the pellet from Berrechid (Fig. 1c,d). Thus, the median differs at most by a factor of three for the DNA quantity and by an even smaller factor of only 1.7 for the fragment size. These differences are not sta-tistically significant (ANOVA P-values of 0.87 and 0.1, respectively, the 0.1 P-value for the fragment size being due to the Mechra Bennabou sample as assessed by pairwise t-tests).

One of these three pellets, that originating from Sidi Chiker, was stored for 26 years in a museum, whereas the two other series of bones where studied within a few weeks following collection of the pellet. This difference in time between collection and analysis does not correspond to obvious differences in DNA preservation, even though we note that no bones containing fragments of an average size above 200 bp were detected in this pellet. This suggests that the long-term conservation in a museum drawer may have caused enough damage to reduce the size of the longest DNA molecules, but, if this was the case, the damage was not sufficient enough to cause a significant median size reduction, indicating that the decay of DNA during digestion by the bird of prey is likely to be the major parameter influencing median DNA lengths. Variation in the extent of DNA decay between pellets was, however, observed when comparing pellets from different birds of prey. Indeed, we also analyzed seven remains from a falcon pellet (F. tinnunuculus) from Ouled Boughadi in Morocco that had been collected a few weeks before analysis and compared them with the remains from the owl pellets. In this case, we could observe a higher extent of DNA degradation than in the owl pellets: the median size was 42 bp, at least 2.5-fold lower than in the owl pellets, and two out of seven bones did not yield the largest amplicon. This difference in the average size is significant (P-value: 0.003 using a t-test for heteroscedastic samples as determined with a Brown-Forsythe test). This higher degradation of DNA in falcon pellets was not unexpected and is probably the result of the lower pH of the gastric juices of falcons (Leprince et al., 1979).

We then explored whether DNA preservation varied between skeletal parts in an attempt to identify specific bones or teeth, which would be more amenable to genetic analyses. No clear difference in DNA quantity or average DNA fragment size was, however, observed in the different types of bones analyzed, that is, femur, tibia, mandible, skull, molars (Fig. 2).
For each type of bone, there were large variations in the quantity of DNA recovered and no clear differences between skeletal parts (Fig. 2a). The values between different bones of the same type were highly variable while the median quantities were not so different for different types of bones or teeth: 9.3 million molecules per gram for long bones, 14.9 million for mandibles and 8.2 million for teeth (Fig. 3b; ANOVA P-value: 0.34). The same trend was observed for the size of preserved DNA molecules (Fig. 2c). We observed high variability in the data, but there was no major difference between bone categories as median size was 139 bp for long bones, 100 bp for mandible and 125 bp for teeth (Fig. 2d, ANOVA P-value: 0.42).

section: dna preservation and degree of digestion
text: We thus sought to analyze whether we could correlate the extent of DNA preservation with some other properties. We first explored microscopic evidence of bone digestion based on the hypothesis that the more acids and enzymes penetrate into the bones and teeth, the less DNA will be preserved. To test this, one half of each of the long bones and mandibles was removed prior to genetic analysis and analyzed through light microscopy and ESEM, to evaluate the degree of damage of surface and histology (Fig. 3c, see also Supporting Information). The microscopic analysis of the skeletal parts revealed that most samples showed little or no digestion on the surface with the exception of one femur head and a mandible that showed moderate digestion. When dividing the samples into three groups (no digestion, light digestion and moderate digestion) as described previously (Andrews, 1990;Fernandez-Jalvo & Andrews, 1992), no correlation could be found between the degree of digestion and both the quantity of initial target DNA molecules and the average size of DNA molecules as determined through qPCR (Fig. 3). Indeed, the median size of DNA molecules and the median DNA content (of a 73 bp fragment) for samples that showed no digestion under the microscope was 106 bp and 12 million molecules per gram, for those showing light digestion it was 100 bp and 6.9 million molecules per gram, and for those showing moderate digestion it was 139 bp and 5.8 million molecules per gram (Fig. 3a,b, two-tailed t-test P-values: 0.95 and 0.83, respectively). Here again, the fluctuation range was found to be high within each category, and there was much more variability between individual bones than between digestion categories. It should be noted that even the most digested samples in this study showed corrosion restricted only to a thin fringe of the most external cortical layer (Fig. 3c, panel iii).

section: dna preservation and exposure to the stomach
text: Finally, we investigated whether the physical position or duration of the bones in the stomach of the bird of prey during the digestion process could influence the extent of DNA preservation. This position and duration cannot be estimated with our dataset, but bones or teeth in anatomical connection are expected to have stayed for the same time and to have been at a similar position within the stomach. We thus compared the quantity of DNA recovered from upper or lower jaw bones with that from the teeth that were still in place within the corresponding jaw bone in the pellet (Fig. 4). Even though there was still some heterogeneity in the amount and length of DNA molecules recovered from connected bones or teeth, grouping based on connection resulted in a lower dispersion of the data. This dataset of connected bones and teeth corresponds to half of the bones analyzed in this study, but it includes 9 out of the 10 samples with the most degraded DNA that did not yield the two largest amplicons. Strikingly, six of these nine samples belonged to only 2 of the 10 groups of connected bones and teeth (Fig. 4b). This uneven distribution of DNA degradation suggests that connected bones/teeth, which have a higher chance of experiencing a similar extent of digestion within the stomach of the bird of prey, indeed showed a similar degree of DNA degradation. A chi-square test of independence reveals that the probability that such an uneven distribution of bones has a 7.6% probability to occur by chance. Thus, even though connected skeletal parts (here teeth in mandibles) have experienced an identical time in the stomach, grouping the bones according to the duration of digestion in the owl's stomach is not sufficient to explain all the variability of the extent of DNA degradation observed. The remaining heterogeneity between bones that experienced a similar digestion time suggests that local factors, such as the position within the stomach, might be another source of variability. section: dna preservation in rodent skeletal parts from pellets and its consequences for genetic analyses
text:
Since pellets of raptors are an excellent source of microvertebrate skeletal material, they could also be a rich and convenient source for phylogenetic and phylogeographic studies, provided DNA is sufficiently preserved. This has been reported to be true in some cases (e.g. Taberlet & Fumagalli, 1996), despite the fact that the skeletal remains of the microvertebrates go through a digestion process inside the stomachs of birds of prey. In order to be able to tap into this genetic resource, it is essential to better characterize the variability of DNA preservation in skeletal parts from pellets, in particular because the same animal may be ejected in two or more different pellets, whereas several individuals, often from different species, may be found within a single pellet (Dodson & Wexlar, 1979). To obtain the most reliable quantitative data, we focused on genetic regions that are abundant and highly conserved between rodents, thus allowing the non- biased generation of data, irrespective of the species of origin. We used the mitochondrial rDNA genes as a proxy to estimate DNA preservation in rodent bones, and focused on the quantitative characterization of the bone-to-bone variability of DNA preservation within a limited number of pellets from the same origin to limit the taphonomic complexity that could be introduced by variable post-deposit environmental conditions. Interestingly, we found the highest degree of variability of DNA preservation to be between the individual skeletal parts, even within the same pellet. We report that both the normalized DNA quantity and the size of the DNA fragments can vary between bones up to two orders of magnitude, while the overall variability of DNA preservation between pellets was found to be lower than threefold. This finding has major implications for future genetic studies using raptor pellets, which rely on multiple genetic markers, irrespective of the analysis method used: multiplex PCR, SNP arrays and/or next-generation sequencing. For multiple marker studies, the pooling of bones from a single pellet will generate sequence mixtures from different skeletal parts likely to contain highly variable states of DNA preservation, in particular concerning the relative quantity of DNA fragments of different sizes. Heterogeneous genetic data from different markers, which estimate the number of individuals based on the relative proportion of different sized products would be a highly error-prone approach. In light of the results of this study, the analysis of individual or connected skeletal parts is a safer alternative for these multiple marker studies.
Because of the large variability in DNA preservation, we stress the importance of using several bones, ideally pre-screening them for DNA preservation using a qPCR-based screening strategy that is adapted to the size and abundance of the genetic markers to be analyzed. Here, we observed that targeting small DNA molecules of 70 bp ensures an amplification success of most (98%) of the samples, whereas only 84% of the samples would be amplified when targeting a 125 bp amplicon. Only a small proportion of the bones contained DNA molecules of higher molecular weight: 7% of the bones contained DNA fragments with an average size larger than 1000 bp, and this corresponded to only a tiny portion of the total DNA present. To select the right amplicon size, it is important to find the proper trade-off between the proportion of samples represented and the effort required to obtain the required amount of genetic information. Targeting smaller amplicons generally requires amplification of multiple PCR products to perform reliable genotyping or phylogenetic analyses. Multiplex PCR would allow achievement of a reasonable compromise between the amount of genetic information obtained and the length of retrievable DNA. Coupling multiplex PCR with next-generation sequencing is likely to be a fruitful approach for efficient genotyping of microvertebrate remains from pellets.
For non-quantitative studies, the use of pooled skeletal remains from single pellets may be sufficient providing the analysis is constrained to a single genetic marker on a single PCR product.

section: possible sources of variability in dna preservation and consequences for sample selection
text:
Since individual or connected skeletal parts turned out to be best suited for genetic analyses, it would be useful to establish proxies to identify the most favorable remains prior to sample screening. We thus explored whether we could identify predictors of DNA preservation. Unfortunately, externally visible features proved to be of little use. Neither the anatomical part considered, nor the microscopic inspection of the extent of digestion could allow identification of a category with better DNA preservation. This is true despite a thorough electron microscopy analysis that identified different degrees of digestion by gastric juices on the surface of different bones. The lack of predictive power of preliminary microscopic observation is probably due to the restriction of microscopically visible corrosion to a thin fringe of the most external cortical layer, which may indicate an overall low level of digestion observed in owl pellet-derived bones analyzed in this study. The best, even though still weak, grouping for the prediction of DNA preservation was obtained when physically connected bones were considered together. Since it has been shown that some remains stay longer in the stomach than others (Dodson & Wexlar, 1979), the duration of exposure to gastric juices could be one of the parameters affecting DNA preservation. The weakness of the correlation suggests, however, other sources of differential DNA degradation during digestion, possibly the position occupied by the skeletal part within the owl stomach or differential protection from gastric juices offered by remaining soft tissue or fur surrounding some bones. Another potential source of variable digestion may also depend on the age of the prey, as younger individuals were reported to be more extensively digested than older ones, possibly due to a lower degree of ossification (Raczynski & Ruprecht, 1974). The variability of the process of bone digestion has previously been reported based on the osteological composition of owl pellets, and several parameters have been invoked such as the amount of damage caused during consumption, the proportion of indigestible elements, the age and species of the raptor and associated pH changes of the gastric juices, and fortuitous movements of bones between the ventriculus and proventriculus (Grimm & Whitehouse, 1963;Raczynski & Ruprecht, 1974). It is likely that these parameters are also involved in the variability of DNA preservation that we observed. The increased correlation observed between DNA preservation and connectedness of skeletal parts suggests local effects regulating exposure to digestive juices, such as position during digestion or protection by the surrounding soft tissue, may account for a large part of the major variation of DNA preservation observed in bones from the same pellet.
To conclude, bones and teeth in pellets of nocturnal, and, to a lesser degree, diurnal birds of prey are a valuable, noninvasive source of DNA of rodents and microvertebrates in general. Their routine use for phylogeographical and genetic studies of microvertebrates can therefore be recommended provided that adequate screening and genetic strategies are used, when necessary, to take into account the highly variable nature of DNA preservation between bones. DNA in skeletal remains is often sufficiently preserved for genetic analyses and any skeletal part can be used for DNA amplification or sequence capture provided small DNA fragments are targeted. This allows for the identification of the species even when only one or few bones are available. The recovery of DNA from partially digested microvertebrate bones and teeth from not only freshly collected pellets, but also recent natural history collections, suggests that some archeological material may also be a suitable DNA source for microvertebrate studies. When experiments are properly designed with respect to the characteristics of DNA preservation presented in this study, the use of raptor pellets as a source for microvertebrate DNA can increase the power of future investigations of microvertebrate phylogeography and ecology.
